problem: The answer says 'Uniaxial moment capacity falls as Pu rises'. That is false over the lower part of the diagram: from pure bending up to the balanced point, Mux1 increases as Pu increases (that is why the interaction curve rises and peaks near the balanced point). The statement only holds above the balanced load.
fix: Mux1 is not constant; it changes with Pu. It rises as Pu increases up to the balanced point and falls beyond it. So capacities read at another Pu describe a different load contour and give a wrong check.

problem: Rectangular-column charts are said to be arranged by b/D ratio. The SP 16 column charts are plotted as Pu/(fck·b·D) against Mu/(fck·b·D²) with lines of p/fck, so they are grouped by concrete grade and by bar arrangement (bars on two sides or on four sides), not by b/D.
fix: Rectangular column charts are normalized, with Pu/(fck·b·D) and Mu/(fck·b·D²) as axes and p/fck as the curve parameter. Choose the chart for the concrete grade and bar layout, then convert back using the actual b and D.

problem: The plotted curve falls steadily from pure compression (0, 1500) to pure bending (160, 0). A real column curve peaks near the balanced point and gives a smaller Mu at Pu = 0 than 130 kN·m, so the shape suggests that the largest moment capacity occurs at zero axial load.
fix: Draw the curve so Mu rises from a low value at Pu = 0 to its maximum near the balanced load, then falls to zero at the pure compression value of Pu, keeping the design point (90, 800) inside.
